title: The shifted geometric mean

blocks.text: A team compares two MILP solvers on its instance set and wants one number per solver, computed the way Hans Mittelmann's benchmark pages define it. For nonnegative values $`v_1, \dots, v_n`$ (solve times, or counts of work) and a shift $`s \ge 0`$:
Write `shifted_geometric_mean(values, shift)` in `sgm.py`, for a nonempty list. The `max(1, ...)` matters: it keeps each logarithm nonnegative, so tiny values cannot pull the mean toward zero.

from __future__ import annotations

import math


def shifted_geometric_mean(values: list[float], shift: float) -> float:
    """exp(mean of ln(max(1, v + shift))) - shift."""
    logs = [math.log(max(1.0, v + shift)) for v in values]
    return math.exp(sum(logs) / len(logs)) - shift


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(shifted_geometric_mean([0.5, 4.0, 120.0], 10.0))

cases.says: with a shift of 0 and values of at least 1, the result is the plain geometric mean
the shift is added to every value and subtracted from the result, so identical values give themselves back
a value plus shift below 1 counts as 1 inside the logarithm
the shift given is the one used, and a larger shift brings two solvers that differ only on fast instances closer together
